statement: Let $F$ be a [finite field](c:finite-field) with $q$ elements. Let $\chi$ be a nontrivial [multiplicative character](c:mul-char), with $\chi(0)=0$, and let $\psi$ be a nontrivial [additive character](c:add-char). Then the [Gauss sum](c:gauss-sum) $G=\sum_{x\in F}\chi(x)\psi(x)$ has $|G|^2=q$. If $\chi^2=1$ on $F^\times$, then $G^2=\chi(-1)\,q$.

hypotheses.text: The set $F$ is a [finite field](c:finite-field) with $q$ elements.
The map $\chi\colon F^\times\to\mathbb{C}^\times$ is a nontrivial [multiplicative character](c:mul-char), extended by $\chi(0)=0$.
The map $\psi\colon (F,+)\to\mathbb{C}^\times$ is a nontrivial [additive character](c:add-char).
For the square formula, $\chi(x)^2=1$ for every nonzero $x$.

conclusion: The [Gauss sum](c:gauss-sum) $G$ has $|G|^2=q$, and $G^2=\chi(-1)\,q$ when $\chi^2=1$.

formal.difference: The declaration states a related product of two Gauss sums, for a character and its inverse. It does not state the magnitude or the square formula.

proofs.name: Character sums and reindexing
proofs.slogan: Expand $|G|^2$ as a double sum, reindex it, and use that the nontrivial character sums vanish.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The square formula uses only that $\chi$ takes the real values $1$ and $-1$.

roles.why: A finite field makes $F$ and $F^\times$ finite groups, so each reindexing map is a bijection of a finite set.
Nontriviality of $\chi$ gives $a$ with $\chi(a)\ne1$, which forces the sum of $\chi$ over $F^\times$ to be $0$.
Nontriviality of $\psi$ gives $z$ with $\psi(z)\ne1$, which forces the sum of $\psi$ over $F$ to be $0$.
Real values of $\chi$ make $\overline{G}=\chi(-1)G$, which turns $|G|^2=q$ into the square formula.

steps.slogan: Show that every nonzero character value has absolute value $1$.
steps.detail: Each value of $\chi$ on $F^\times$ and of $\psi$ on $F$ lies in a finite group, so it is a root of unity. Hence $|\chi(x)|=1$ for $x\ne0$ and $|\psi(x)|=1$ for all $x$. The complex conjugate of each value is its inverse.

steps.slogan: Prove by reindexing that the sums of the nontrivial characters vanish.
steps.detail: Choose $a$ with $\chi(a)\ne1$. The bijection $x\mapsto ax$ gives $\sum_{F^\times}\chi=\chi(a)\sum_{F^\times}\chi$, so this sum is $0$. In the same way, $\sum_{F}\psi=0$. Hence $\sum_{y\in F^\times}\psi(by)=-1$ for $b\ne0$ and $q-1$ for $b=0$.

steps.slogan: Expand $|G|^2$ as a double sum and substitute $x=ty$ for $y\ne0$.
steps.detail: Write $|G|^2=G\overline{G}$ as a finite double sum. The terms with $x=0$ or $y=0$ vanish. For $y\ne0$, the bijection $x=ty$ gives $|G|^2=\sum_{t\in F^\times}\chi(t)\sum_{y\in F^\times}\psi((t-1)y)$.

steps.slogan: Split off the term $t=1$ and sum the remaining terms to get $q$.
steps.detail: The term $t=1$ has inner sum $q-1$ and $\chi(1)=1$. Every other $t$ contributes $-\chi(t)$, and $\sum_{t\ne0,1}\chi(t)=-1$. Hence $|G|^2=(q-1)+1=q$.

steps.slogan: Compare $\overline{G}$ with $G$ for a real character to get the square.
steps.detail: If $\chi^2=1$, all values of $\chi$ are $\pm1$, so $\overline{G}=\sum\chi(x)\psi(-x)$. Replace $x$ by $-x$ to get $\overline{G}=\chi(-1)G$. Then $\chi(-1)G^2=q$, and $\chi(-1)^2=1$ gives $G^2=\chi(-1)q$.

concepts.c:finite-field: Finiteness makes the sums finite and the reindexing maps bijections.
concepts.c:mul-char: Nontriviality of the multiplicative character gives a zero sum over the units.
concepts.c:add-char: Nontriviality of the additive character gives zero sums that fix the inner sum.
concepts.c:gauss-sum: The proof computes the absolute value and the square of this sum.

statement: Let $H_n$ be the [Hermite polynomials](c:hermite-polynomial) with $H_0=1$ and $H_{n+1}(x)=xH_n(x)-H_n'(x)$. For integers $m,n\ge0$, the integral $\int_{\mathbb{R}}H_mH_ne^{-x^2/2}\,dx$ converges absolutely. It equals $\sqrt{2\pi}\,n!$ if $m=n$ and $0$ otherwise.

hypotheses.text: The [Hermite polynomials](c:hermite-polynomial) $H_n$ satisfy $H_0=1$ and $H_{n+1}(x)=xH_n(x)-H_n'(x)$.
The indices $m$ and $n$ are integers with $m,n\ge0$.
The weight is $e^{-x^2/2}$, and the integral is the [Lebesgue integral](c:lebesgue-integral) on $\mathbb{R}$.

conclusion: Each integral converges absolutely, and its value is $\sqrt{2\pi}\,n!$ for $m=n$ and $0$ for $m\ne n$.

formal.difference: The declaration states the Rodrigues formula $\varphi^{(n)}=(-1)^nH_n\varphi$ for the Gaussian weight. It does not state orthogonality.

proofs.name: Rodrigues formula and integration by parts
proofs.slogan: Write $H_n\varphi$ as an $n$-th derivative of the Gaussian, integrate by parts $n$ times, and differentiate $H_m$.
proofs.scope: All pairs $m,n\ge0$. The case $m<n$ follows from the case $m>n$ by symmetry of the product.

roles.why: The recursion gives the degree and leading coefficient of $H_n$, and the Rodrigues formula by induction.
The indices fix how many times to integrate by parts and which case of $m$ and $n$ applies.
The Gaussian weight makes every polynomial integrable and kills the boundary terms.

steps.slogan: Show by induction that $H_n$ is monic of degree $n$.
steps.detail: The term $xH_n$ has degree $n+1$ and leading coefficient $1$. The derivative $H_n'$ has smaller degree, so subtraction does not change the leading term.

steps.slogan: Prove by induction that the $n$-th derivative of $\varphi=e^{-x^2/2}$ is $(-1)^nH_n\varphi$.
steps.detail: The case $n=0$ is clear. Since $\varphi'=-x\varphi$, the product rule gives $D\big((-1)^nH_n\varphi\big)=(-1)^n(H_n'-xH_n)\varphi=(-1)^{n+1}H_{n+1}\varphi$.

steps.slogan: Show that each polynomial times $\varphi$ is integrable and tends to $0$ at infinity.
steps.detail: For large $|x|$, $k\log|x|\le x^2/4$, so $|x|^k\varphi(x)\le e^{-x^2/4}$. The [Gaussian integral](c:gaussian-integral) shows that this bound is integrable. The same bound gives the limit $0$ at $\pm\infty$.

steps.slogan: Integrate $H_m\varphi^{(n)}$ by parts $n$ times and drop the boundary terms.
steps.detail: On a finite interval, each integration by parts moves one derivative onto $H_m$. Send both endpoints to infinity: every boundary term is a [polynomial](c:polynomial) times $\varphi$, so it vanishes. The signs $(-1)^n$ cancel, so $\int H_mH_n\varphi=\int H_m^{(n)}\varphi$.

steps.slogan: Evaluate $\int H_m^{(n)}\varphi$ for $n>m$, for $n=m$, and by symmetry for $n<m$.
steps.detail: If $n>m$, then $H_m^{(n)}=0$ and the integral is $0$. If $n=m$, monicity gives $H_n^{(n)}=n!$, and the Gaussian integral gives $n!\sqrt{2\pi}$. If $n<m$, swap $m$ and $n$ in the product.

concepts.c:hermite-polynomial: The recursion defines the polynomials whose degree and derivatives the proof tracks.
concepts.c:lebesgue-integral: Absolute integrability lets the improper limits and integration by parts stand.
concepts.c:gaussian-integral: The integral of the Gaussian supplies the bound and the value $\sqrt{2\pi}$.
concepts.c:polynomial: A polynomial times the Gaussian is integrable and vanishes at infinity.

statement: Let $P$ be a [p-group](c:p-group) of order $p^n$ that acts on a finite set $X$. Let $X^P$ be the set of points fixed by every element of $P$. Then $|X|\equiv|X^P| \pmod p$. If $n\ge1$, then $p$ divides the order of the [center](c:center) $Z(P)$, so $Z(P)$ is not trivial.

hypotheses.text: The group $P$ is a finite [p-group](c:p-group) of order $p^n$ for a prime $p$.
The group $P$ acts by permutations on the finite set $X$ (a [group action](c:group-action)).
For the claim about the center, $n\ge1$.

conclusion: The congruence $|X|\equiv|X^P|\pmod p$ holds, and $p$ divides $|Z(P)|$ when $n\ge1$.

formal.difference: The declaration states the congruence only. The claim about the center is a consequence that it does not state.

proofs.name: Orbit counting
proofs.slogan: Split $X$ into orbits of $p$-power size, then apply the congruence to the conjugation action on $P$.
proofs.scope: The whole statement. The case $n=0$ has $Z(P)=P$ trivial, so only the congruence is claimed there.

roles.why: The order $p^n$ makes every [orbit](c:orbit) size a power of $p$, and gives $p\mid|P|$ for $n\ge1$.
The action splits $X$ into orbits, and the conjugation action identifies the fixed points with the center.
The condition $n\ge1$ gives $p\mid|P|$, which transfers to $|Z(P)|$.

steps.slogan: Show that each [orbit](c:orbit) has a size that divides $|P|$, so it is a power of $p$.
steps.detail: For $x\in X$ with stabilizer $P_x$, the map $gP_x\mapsto g\cdot x$ is a bijection from the cosets of $P_x$ onto the orbit of $x$. So the orbit size times $|P_x|$ equals $|P|=p^n$. An orbit has size $1$ if and only if its point is fixed, and every other orbit has size divisible by $p$.

steps.slogan: Add the orbit sizes of $X$ to get $|X|\equiv|X^P|$ modulo $p$.
steps.detail: The orbits partition $X$. The orbits of size $1$ are the points of $X^P$, and all other orbits have sizes divisible by $p$. So $|X|=|X^P|+$ a multiple of $p$.

steps.slogan: Let $P$ act on the set $P$ by conjugation and identify its fixed points with the center.
steps.detail: With $g\cdot x=gxg^{-1}$, a point $x$ is fixed if and only if it commutes with every $g$. So $X^P=Z(P)$ for this action.

steps.slogan: Apply the congruence to this action to show that $p$ divides $|Z(P)|$.
steps.detail: The congruence gives $|P|\equiv|Z(P)|\pmod p$. For $n\ge1$, $p$ divides $|P|$, so $p$ divides $|Z(P)|$. The identity lies in $Z(P)$, so $|Z(P)|\ge p\ge2$ and $Z(P)$ is not trivial.

concepts.c:p-group: The order $p^n$ forces orbit sizes to be powers of $p$.
concepts.c:group-action: The action partitions the set into orbits that the proof counts.
concepts.c:orbit: Orbit sizes divide the group order, and size $1$ means a fixed point.
concepts.c:center: The center is the fixed point set of the conjugation action.

statement: Let $G$ be a finite group of automorphisms of a field $F$. Let $K=F^G$ be the subfield of elements fixed by every element of $G$. Then $F$ is a finite [field extension](c:field-extension) of $K$, and its [degree](c:degree-of-an-extension) is $[F:K]=|G|$.

hypotheses.text: The group $G$ is finite, with $|G|=n$.
Each element of $G$ is an automorphism of the field $F$, and distinct elements are distinct maps.

conclusion: $F$ is a finite extension of $F^G$ with $[F:F^G]=|G|$.

formal.difference: The declaration states the equality for the dimension of $F$ over the fixed subfield, for a finite group that acts faithfully. It is a related form of the statement.

proofs.name: Linear systems and independence of characters
proofs.slogan: Bound the degree above with a solution of least support, and below with the independence of the automorphisms.
proofs.scope: The two inequalities $[F:K]\le n$ and $[F:K]\ge n$, which together give equality and finiteness.

roles.why: Finiteness of $G$ gives a system with $n$ equations, and a permutation of those equations by each $g$.
Distinct automorphisms are the characters whose [linear independence](c:linear-independence) gives the lower bound.

steps.slogan: Take $m>n$ elements independent over $K$ and solve $n$ equations in $m$ unknowns.
steps.detail: Let $x_1,\dots,x_m\in F$ be [linearly independent](c:linear-independence) over $K$ with $m>n$. The equations $\sum_j g_i(x_j)y_j=0$ for $i=1,\dots,n$ have fewer equations than unknowns. So a nonzero solution exists in $F$.

steps.slogan: Choose a solution of least support and show that all its entries lie in $K$.
steps.detail: Scale a nonzero solution with the fewest nonzero entries so that one entry is $1$. Applying $g\in G$ permutes the equations, so $g(y)$ is a solution with the same support. Then $y-g(y)$ has smaller support, so it is $0$. Hence every $y_j$ is fixed by $G$.

steps.slogan: Read the equation of the identity to contradict independence, so $[F:K]\le n$.
steps.detail: The equation for $g=\mathrm{id}$ is $\sum_jx_jy_j=0$ with $y_j\in K$ not all zero. This contradicts the independence of the $x_j$ over $K$.

steps.slogan: Suppose $[F:K]=m<n$ and turn a nonzero solution into a relation among the $g_i$.
steps.detail: Let $x_1,\dots,x_m$ be a $K$-basis of $F$. The $m$ equations $\sum_ig_i(x_j)y_i=0$ in $n$ unknowns have a nonzero solution. Every $a\in F$ is a $K$-combination of the $x_j$, and each coefficient is fixed by every $g_i$. So $\sum_iy_ig_i(a)=0$ for all $a$.

steps.slogan: Contradict the independence of the $n$ distinct automorphisms to get $[F:K]\ge n$.
steps.detail: The relation $\sum_iy_ig_i=0$ on $F$ is nontrivial, and $g_1,\dots,g_n$ are distinct. This contradicts the independence of characters. So $m<n$ is false.

steps.slogan: Combine the two bounds to get $[F:K]=n=|G|$.
steps.detail: The upper bound shows that no more than $n$ elements are independent, so $F$ is a finite extension of $K$. The lower bound shows that the degree is at least $n$.

concepts.c:field-extension: The theorem states that the fixed field has a finite extension $F$.
concepts.c:degree-of-an-extension: The degree is the dimension that both bounds compare with $n$.
concepts.c:linear-independence: Independence of elements and of automorphisms drives both bounds.

statement: Let $F$ be a [field](c:field) and let $f\in F[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ be a [polynomial](c:polynomial) of [total degree](c:total-degree) $t_1+\dots+t_n$. Assume that the coefficient of $x_1^{t_1}\cdots x_n^{t_n}$ is nonzero. Let $S_i\subseteq F$ be finite sets with $|S_i|>t_i$. Then $f(s)\ne0$ for some $s\in S_1\times\dots\times S_n$.

hypotheses.text: The polynomial $f$ has [total degree](c:total-degree) exactly $t_1+\dots+t_n$.
The coefficient of $x_1^{t_1}\cdots x_n^{t_n}$ in $f$ is nonzero.
Each $S_i$ is a finite subset of the [field](c:field) $F$ with $|S_i|>t_i$.

conclusion: Some point $s\in S_1\times\dots\times S_n$ has $f(s)\ne0$.

formal.difference: The declaration is the mathlib form of this result. Its hypotheses and its notation for the degree condition may differ from this statement.

proofs.name: Reduction modulo the grid polynomials
proofs.slogan: Reduce $f$ modulo the polynomials that vanish on the grid, keep the top coefficient, and apply a zero lemma.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The proof shrinks each $S_i$ to exactly $t_i+1$ elements and argues by contradiction.

roles.why: The degree bound makes each quotient small, so division does not change the coefficient of the top monomial.
The nonzero coefficient survives in the remainder, so the remainder is not the zero polynomial.
The sizes $|S_i|>t_i$ give the grid polynomials and the root count in the zero lemma.

steps.slogan: Shrink each $S_i$ to $t_i+1$ elements and assume that $f$ vanishes on the grid.
steps.detail: A point found in a smaller grid lies in the larger grid, so assume $|S_i|=t_i+1$. Put $g_i(x_i)=\prod_{s\in S_i}(x_i-s)$. It is monic of degree $t_i+1$ and vanishes on $S_i$. Suppose that $f$ vanishes at every grid point.

steps.slogan: Divide $f$ by $g_1,\dots,g_n$ in turn to get a remainder of degree at most $t_i$ in $x_i$.
steps.detail: Divide by $g_1$ in $x_1$, then by $g_2$ in $x_2$, and so on. This gives $f=\sum h_ig_i+r$ with $\deg_{x_i}r\le t_i$. Each division keeps the total degree at most $\deg f$, and $h_i$ has total degree at most $\deg f-(t_i+1)$.

steps.slogan: Show that the remainder $r$ has the same nonzero coefficient at $x^t$ as $f$.
steps.detail: The top-degree part of $h_ig_i$ is the top part of $h_i$ times $x_i^{t_i+1}$. Every monomial in it has $x_i$-exponent at least $t_i+1$. The monomial $x^t$ has exponent $t_i$, so it does not occur in $h_ig_i$.

steps.slogan: Show that $r$ vanishes at every point of the grid.
steps.detail: At a grid point, $f=0$ by assumption and each $g_i=0$. So $r=f-\sum h_ig_i$ is $0$ there.

steps.slogan: Prove by induction on $n$ that a remainder that vanishes on the grid is zero.
steps.detail: Write $r=\sum_{k\le t_n}c_k(x_1,\dots,x_{n-1})x_n^k$. At a fixed point of the smaller grid, the one-variable polynomial in $x_n$ has degree at most $t_n$ and at least $t_n+1$ roots, so it is $0$. So each $c_k$ vanishes on the smaller grid, and induction gives $c_k=0$.

steps.slogan: Compare $r=0$ with the nonzero coefficient of $x^t$ to reach a contradiction.
steps.detail: The zero lemma gives $r=0$. This contradicts the nonzero coefficient of $x^t$ in $r$. So $f$ does not vanish on the whole grid.

concepts.c:field: A field has no zero divisors, so a nonzero polynomial in one variable has few roots.
concepts.c:polynomial: The proof divides polynomials and compares their monomials.
concepts.c:total-degree: The total degree bounds the quotients and keeps the top coefficient.

statement: Let $S^1=\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ with base point $x_0=[0]$. Each loop $\gamma$ at $x_0$ has a unique lift $\tilde\gamma$ to $\mathbb{R}$ with $\tilde\gamma(0)=0$. The [winding number](c:winding-number) $w(\gamma)=\tilde\gamma(1)$ is an integer, and $w$ is a group isomorphism from the [fundamental group](c:fundamental-group) $\pi_1(S^1,x_0)$ onto $\mathbb{Z}$.

hypotheses.text: The loops are continuous maps $\gamma\colon[0,1]\to S^1$ with $\gamma(0)=\gamma(1)=x_0$ on the [circle](c:circle).
Homotopies of loops keep the base point fixed at every time.
The group operation of the [fundamental group](c:fundamental-group) is concatenation of loops.

conclusion: The number $w(\gamma)$ depends only on the homotopy class, and $w$ is a bijective homomorphism. So two loops are homotopic relative to $x_0$ if and only if their winding numbers are equal. The inverse sends $n$ to the class of $t\mapsto nt \bmod 1$.

formal.difference: The declaration is a neighbouring mathlib fact. It states a related or smaller result in the form that mathlib uses.

proofs.name: Lifting to the covering space
proofs.slogan: Lift loops and homotopies to the covering space $\mathbb{R}$ and read the end point of the lift as an integer.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. Every claim uses the covering map $\mathbb{R}\to S^1$ with fiber $\mathbb{Z}$.

roles.why: A loop lifts to a path in $\mathbb{R}$ that starts at $0$ and ends in the fiber $\mathbb{Z}$.
A homotopy that fixes the base point lifts to a map whose end points lie in the discrete fiber, so they stay constant.
Concatenation of loops becomes concatenation of lifts, which adds the end points.

steps.slogan: Lift each loop and each homotopy uniquely to the [covering space](c:covering-space) $\mathbb{R}$.
steps.detail: The quotient map $\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ is a covering map with fiber $\mathbb{Z}$. Path lifting and the homotopy lifting property give unique lifts with a given start. The end point $\tilde\gamma(1)$ lies in the fiber over $x_0$, so $w(\gamma)\in\mathbb{Z}$.

steps.slogan: Show that homotopic loops have equal winding numbers, so $w$ is defined on classes.
steps.detail: Lift a homotopy $H$ from $\gamma$ to $\gamma'$ with $\tilde H(0,0)=0$. The edge paths are lifts of $\gamma$, of $\gamma'$ and of the constant path, so uniqueness identifies them. The map $s\mapsto\tilde H(s,1)$ is continuous with values in the discrete fiber $\mathbb{Z}$, so it is constant. Hence $\tilde\gamma(1)=\tilde\gamma'(1)$.

steps.slogan: Show that the lift of a concatenation adds the winding numbers.
steps.detail: If $w(\gamma)=a$ and $w(\delta)=b$, the lift of $\gamma\cdot\delta$ is $\tilde\gamma$ followed by $\tilde\delta$ shifted by $a$. It starts at $0$ and ends at $a+b$. So $w(\gamma\cdot\delta)=a+b$.

steps.slogan: Show that the loop $t\mapsto nt \bmod 1$ has winding number $n$.
steps.detail: The loop $\omega_n(t)=nt \bmod 1$ has the lift $t\mapsto nt$ by uniqueness. Its end point is $n$, so $w(\omega_n)=n$.

steps.slogan: Join two lifts with the same end point by a straight-line homotopy.
steps.detail: Let $w(\gamma)=w(\gamma')$. The lifts $\tilde\gamma$ and $\tilde\gamma'$ are paths in $\mathbb{R}$ from $0$ to one integer. The homotopy $(1-s)\tilde\gamma+s\tilde\gamma'$ fixes both ends. Its image in $S^1$ is a homotopy at $x_0$ from $\gamma$ to $\gamma'$.

steps.slogan: Combine the homomorphism, the surjection and the injection into an isomorphism.
steps.detail: The map $w$ is a homomorphism, it is onto $\mathbb{Z}$, and it is one to one on classes. So it is an isomorphism with inverse $n\mapsto[\omega_n]$.

concepts.c:winding-number: The winding number is the integer end point of the lift.
concepts.c:fundamental-group: The proof identifies this group with the integers.
concepts.c:covering-space: The covering map gives unique lifts and a discrete fiber.
concepts.c:circle: The circle is the base space of the covering map from the real line.

statement: Let $E$ be a real [normed space](c:norm). Let $f\colon[a,b]\to E$ and $B\colon[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and [differentiable](c:differentiable-function) on $(a,b)$, with $\|f'(t)\|\le B'(t)$ on $(a,b)$. Then $\|f(b)-f(a)\|\le B(b)-B(a)$. If $\|f'\|\le M$, then $\|f(b)-f(a)\|\le M(b-a)$.

hypotheses.text: The space $E$ is a real [normed space](c:norm).
The maps $f$ and $B$ are continuous on $[a,b]$ and [differentiable](c:differentiable-function) on $(a,b)$.
The inequality $\|f'(t)\|\le B'(t)$ holds for all $t\in(a,b)$.

conclusion: $\|f(b)-f(a)\|\le B(b)-B(a)$, and $\|f(b)-f(a)\|\le M(b-a)$ when $\|f'\|\le M$.

formal.difference: The declaration is a neighbouring mathlib fact. It states a related or smaller result in the form that mathlib uses.

proofs.name: Norming functional
proofs.slogan: Pair $f$ with a norming functional to reduce to a real function, then apply the scalar mean value theorem.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The case $f(b)=f(a)$ is separate because a norming functional needs a nonzero vector.

roles.why: The norm gives a continuous linear functional $\varphi$ of norm at most $1$ with $\varphi(v)=\|v\|$.
Continuity and differentiability make $\varphi\circ f-B$ a real function that satisfies the mean value theorem.
The bound $\|f'\|\le B'$ makes the derivative of the real function nonpositive and shows that $B$ does not decrease.

steps.slogan: Treat the case $f(b)=f(a)$ by showing that $B$ does not decrease.
steps.detail: If $v=f(b)-f(a)=0$, the claim needs $B(b)\ge B(a)$. This holds because $B'\ge\|f'\|\ge0$ on $(a,b)$, so $B$ is nondecreasing by the scalar mean value theorem.

steps.slogan: Choose a norming functional $\varphi$ on $E$ with $\|\varphi\|\le1$ and $\varphi(v)=\|v\|$.
steps.detail: Let $v=f(b)-f(a)\ne0$. The Hahn-Banach theorem gives a continuous linear $\varphi\colon E\to\mathbb{R}$ in the [dual space](c:dual-space) with $\|\varphi\|\le1$ and $\varphi(v)=\|v\|$.

steps.slogan: Form the real function $h=\varphi\circ f-B$ and show that $h'\le0$.
steps.detail: The function $h$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. A continuous linear map commutes with the derivative, so $h'=\varphi(f')-B'$. Since $\|\varphi\|\le1$, $\varphi(f'(t))\le\|f'(t)\|\le B'(t)$, so $h'\le0$.

steps.slogan: Apply the scalar mean value theorem to $h$ to get $h(b)\le h(a)$.
steps.detail: The function $h$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable inside. There is $\xi\in(a,b)$ with $h(b)-h(a)=h'(\xi)(b-a)\le0$. So $\varphi(f(b))-\varphi(f(a))\le B(b)-B(a)$.

steps.slogan: Read off the inequality, then take $B(t)=Mt$ for a constant bound.
steps.detail: The left side equals $\varphi(v)=\|v\|$, so $\|f(b)-f(a)\|\le B(b)-B(a)$. For $\|f'\|\le M$, put $B(t)=Mt$. Then $B'=M$ and $B(b)-B(a)=M(b-a)$.

concepts.c:norm: The norm defines the size that the inequality bounds and the norming functional.
concepts.c:differentiable-function: Differentiability on the open interval lets the mean value theorem apply.
concepts.c:dual-space: The norming functional is an element of the dual space.

statement: Let $B_n$ be the [Bernoulli numbers](c:bernoulli-number), defined by $t/(e^t-1)=\sum_{n\ge0}B_nt^n/n!$. For every integer $k\ge1$, the [zeta value](c:riemann-zeta-function) is $\zeta(2k)=(-1)^{k+1}(2\pi)^{2k}B_{2k}/\big(2\,(2k)!\big)$. So $\zeta(2k)/\pi^{2k}$ is rational, and $B_{2k}$ has the sign $(-1)^{k+1}$.

hypotheses.text: The number $k$ is an integer with $k\ge1$.
The [Bernoulli numbers](c:bernoulli-number) come from the series of $t/(e^t-1)$, so $B_1=-1/2$.
The [power series](c:power-series) identities hold for $|z|<1$, the largest disc about $0$ with no pole of $\cot\pi z$ other than $0$.

conclusion: $\zeta(2k)=(-1)^{k+1}(2\pi)^{2k}B_{2k}/\big(2\,(2k)!\big)$, so $\zeta(2k)/\pi^{2k}$ is rational and $B_{2k}$ has sign $(-1)^{k+1}$.

proofs.name: Two series for the cotangent
proofs.slogan: Expand $\pi z\cot\pi z$ as a power series in two ways, with Bernoulli numbers and with zeta values, and compare the coefficients.
proofs.scope: All $k\ge1$. The sign of $B_{2k}$ follows from $\zeta(2k)>0$. The identity for $\pi z\cot\pi z$ is proved on $|z|<1$.

roles.why: Each index $k\ge1$ picks the coefficient of $z^{2k}$ to compare.
The definition by $t/(e^t-1)$ gives the Taylor coefficients $B_n/n!$ and, with $B_1=-1/2$, the even function $\varphi(t)+t/2$.
On $|z|<1$ both expansions converge absolutely, so the sums can be swapped and the coefficients compared.

steps.slogan: Show that $t/(e^t-1)+t/2$ is an even function with a series on $|t|<2\pi$.
steps.detail: The function $\varphi(t)=t/(e^t-1)$ with $\varphi(0)=1$ is holomorphic for $|t|<2\pi$, because the zeros of $e^t-1$ are the points $2\pi im$. Its Taylor coefficients are $B_n/n!$. The sum $\varphi(t)+t/2=(t/2)\coth(t/2)$ is even. So $B_1=-1/2$ and $B_n=0$ for odd $n\ge3$.

steps.slogan: Put $t=2i\pi z$ to expand $\pi z\cot\pi z$ with the Bernoulli numbers.
steps.detail: With $t=2iu$, $(t/2)\coth(t/2)=u\cot u$. The even series gives $u\cot u=\sum_{k\ge0}(-1)^kB_{2k}(2u)^{2k}/(2k)!$ for $|u|<\pi$. Put $u=\pi z$ to get $\pi z\cot\pi z=\sum_{k\ge0}(-1)^kB_{2k}(2\pi z)^{2k}/(2k)!$ for $|z|<1$.

steps.slogan: Expand $\pi z\cot\pi z$ again from its partial fractions as a series in $\zeta(2k)$.
steps.detail: The partial fraction expansion gives $\pi z\cot\pi z=1+\sum_{n\ge1}2z^2/(z^2-n^2)$. For $|z|<1$, $2z^2/(z^2-n^2)=-2\sum_{k\ge1}(z/n)^{2k}$. The double series converges absolutely, so the sums can be swapped. This gives $\pi z\cot\pi z=1-2\sum_{k\ge1}\zeta(2k)z^{2k}$.

steps.slogan: Equate the coefficients of the two power series and solve for $\zeta(2k)$.
steps.detail: Two power series that agree on $|z|<1$ have equal coefficients. For $k\ge1$ this gives $-2\zeta(2k)=(-1)^kB_{2k}(2\pi)^{2k}/(2k)!$. Solve for $\zeta(2k)$.

steps.slogan: Read off the rationality of $\zeta(2k)/\pi^{2k}$ and the sign of $B_{2k}$.
steps.detail: The formula gives $\zeta(2k)/\pi^{2k}=(-1)^{k+1}2^{2k-1}B_{2k}/(2k)!$, which is rational. Since $\zeta(2k)>0$, the sign of $B_{2k}$ is $(-1)^{k+1}$.

concepts.c:bernoulli-number: The Bernoulli numbers are the Taylor coefficients of $t/(e^t-1)$ and appear in the answer.
concepts.c:riemann-zeta-function: The zeta values are the coefficients of the second expansion.
concepts.c:power-series: Equality of two power series on a disc gives equal coefficients.

statement: Let $f,g\colon\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{C}$ and $(f*g)(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}f(d)g(n/d)$. If the [Dirichlet series](c:dirichlet-series) of $f$ and $g$ converge absolutely at $s$, then that of $f*g$ does too, and $L(f*g,s)=L(f,s)L(g,s)$. Hence $1/\zeta(s)=\sum\mu(n)n^{-s}$ for $\operatorname{Re}s>1$, and the density of [coprime](c:coprime-integers) pairs is $1/\zeta(2)=6/\pi^2$.

hypotheses.text: The [Dirichlet series](c:dirichlet-series) $L(f,s)=\sum f(n)n^{-s}$ and $L(g,s)$ converge absolutely at $s$, and only $n\ge1$ counts.
For the consequences, $\operatorname{Re}s>1$ and $\mu$ is the Möbius function, with $\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d)=1$ for $n=1$ and $0$ for $n>1$.

conclusion: $L(f*g,s)$ converges absolutely and equals $L(f,s)L(g,s)$. Also $1/\zeta(s)=\sum\mu(n)n^{-s}$ for $\operatorname{Re}s>1$, and the density of coprime pairs is $6/\pi^2$.

proofs.name: Double series and Möbius function
proofs.slogan: Multiply the two series, regroup the absolutely convergent double series by $n=ab$, then specialize to $\mu$ and the constant $1$.
proofs.scope: The product formula for all $f,g$ with absolute convergence, and its two consequences for $\operatorname{Re}s>1$.

roles.why: Absolute convergence lets the double series be summed in any order and grouped by the product $ab$.
The Möbius identity gives $\mu*1=\delta$ and the indicator of coprimality, which yield $1/\zeta$ and the density.

steps.slogan: Write $L(f,s)L(g,s)$ as a double series and show that it converges absolutely.
steps.detail: The product equals $\sum_{a,b\ge1}f(a)g(b)(ab)^{-s}$. With $\sigma=\operatorname{Re}s$, the sum of the absolute values is $\big(\sum|f(a)|a^{-\sigma}\big)\big(\sum|g(b)|b^{-\sigma}\big)<\infty$. So the terms may be summed in any order.

steps.slogan: Group the terms by $n=ab$ to get the series of $f*g$.
steps.detail: The terms with $ab=n$ add to $(f*g)(n)n^{-s}$. So $L(f,s)L(g,s)=L(f*g,s)$. The same grouping for $|f|$ and $|g|$ shows absolute convergence, because $|f*g|\le|f|*|g|.

steps.slogan: Take $f=\mu$ and $g=1$ to show that $1/\zeta(s)=\sum\mu(n)n^{-s}$.
steps.detail: The Möbius property says $\mu*1=\delta$, where $\delta(1)=1$ and $\delta(n)=0$ otherwise. The product formula gives $L(\mu,s)\zeta(s)=1$ for $\operatorname{Re}s>1$.

steps.slogan: Count the [coprime](c:coprime-integers) pairs in $[1,N]^2$ with the Möbius sum.
steps.detail: For $a,b\in[1,N]$, $[\gcd(a,b)=1]=\sum_{k\mid\gcd(a,b)}\mu(k)$. There are $\lfloor N/k\rfloor$ multiples of $k$ in $[1,N]$. So the number of coprime pairs is $C(N)=\sum_{k\le N}\mu(k)\lfloor N/k\rfloor^2$.

steps.slogan: Let $N\to\infty$ to get the density $1/\zeta(2)=6/\pi^2$.
steps.detail: Since $\lfloor N/k\rfloor^2=N^2/k^2+O(N/k)$, we get $C(N)/N^2=\sum_{k\le N}\mu(k)/k^2+O(\ln N/N)$. The sum tends to $L(\mu,2)=1/\zeta(2)=6/\pi^2$.

concepts.c:dirichlet-series: The theorem is an identity between three Dirichlet series.
concepts.c:coprime-integers: Coprimality is the condition that the Möbius sum detects.

statement: Assume the [axiom of choice](c:axiom-of-choice). If $X$ is an [infinite set](c:infinite-set), there is a bijection $X\times X\to X$, so $\kappa\cdot\kappa=\kappa$ for every infinite [cardinal](c:cardinal-number) $\kappa$. Hence $\kappa+\lambda=\kappa\cdot\lambda=\kappa$ for $1\le\lambda\le\kappa$, the finite sequences in $X$ have cardinality $|X|$, and $|K[x]|=|K|$ for an infinite field $K$.

hypotheses.text: The [axiom of choice](c:axiom-of-choice) holds, used through Zorn's lemma and the comparability of cardinals.
The set $X$ is [infinite](c:infinite-set), so it has a [countably infinite](c:countable-set) subset.

conclusion: A bijection $X\times X\to X$ exists, so $\kappa\cdot\kappa=\kappa$. The sums, the products, the finite sequences and the polynomial ring follow.

formal.difference: The declaration states $\kappa\cdot\kappa=\kappa$ for an infinite cardinal. It is a smaller fact than this statement, which adds the consequences.

proofs.name: Zorn's lemma on partial pairings
proofs.slogan: Order the partial pairing bijections, take a maximal one by Zorn's lemma, and show that it covers almost all of $X$.
proofs.scope: The whole statement. The core is $|X\times X|=|X|$ for infinite $X$; the consequences follow by short cardinal arithmetic.

roles.why: The axiom of choice gives Zorn's lemma and the comparability of cardinals that the proof uses.
An infinite set holds a countably infinite subset, which starts the order, and the argument never leaves the infinite case.

steps.slogan: Order the pairs $(A,f)$, with $f\colon A\times A\to A$ a bijection, by extension.
steps.detail: Let $S$ be the set of pairs with $A\subseteq X$ infinite. Set $(A,f)\le(A',f')$ if $A\subseteq A'$ and $f'$ restricts to $f$. A [countably infinite](c:countable-set) $A_0\subseteq X$ with the Cantor pairing shows that $S$ is not empty.

steps.slogan: Show that every chain has an upper bound and take a maximal pair $(A,f)$.
steps.detail: For a chain $(A_i,f_i)$, put $A=\bigcup A_i$ and $f=\bigcup f_i$. Two points of $A$ lie in one $A_i$, so $f$ is a well defined injective map onto $A$. Zorn's lemma gives a maximal element.

steps.slogan: Show by contradiction that the complement of $A$ is smaller than $A$.
steps.detail: Suppose $|A|\le|X\setminus A|$ by comparability. Choose $B\subseteq X\setminus A$ with $|B|=|A|$. The set $D=(A\times B)\cup(B\times A)\cup(B\times B)$ has size $3|A|=|A|=|B|$, so a bijection $h\colon D\to B$ exists. Then $f\cup h$ is a bijection on $A\cup B$, which contradicts maximality.

steps.slogan: Compare $|X|$ with $|A|$ to get $|X\times X|=|X|$.
steps.detail: Now $|A|\le|X|=|A|+|X\setminus A|\le2|A|=|A|$, so $|X|=|A|$ by the Schröder-Bernstein theorem. Then $X\times X$, $A\times A$, $A$ and $X$ have the same size.

steps.slogan: Derive the sums, the finite sequences and the polynomial ring from $\kappa\cdot\kappa=\kappa$.
steps.detail: For $1\le\lambda\le\kappa$, $\kappa\le\kappa+\lambda\le\kappa\cdot\kappa=\kappa$, and the same bound holds for the product. By induction $|X^n|=|X|$, so $|X^{<\omega}|\le\aleph_0\cdot|X|=|X|$. A polynomial over $K$ is a finite sequence of coefficients, so $|K[x]|=|K|$.

concepts.c:axiom-of-choice: Choice supplies Zorn's lemma and the comparison of two cardinals.
concepts.c:infinite-set: The theorem holds for infinite sets only.
concepts.c:cardinal-number: The statement is an equation between cardinal numbers.
concepts.c:countable-set: A countably infinite subset starts the order of partial pairings.

statement: If two finite Borel measures $\mu,\nu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ have equal [characteristic functions](c:characteristic-function), then $\mu=\nu$. Random vectors $X,Y$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$ are [independent](c:independent-random-variables) if and only if $\mathbb{E}\,e^{i\langle s,X\rangle+i\langle t,Y\rangle}=\varphi_X(s)\varphi_Y(t)$ for all $s,t\in\mathbb{R}^d$.

hypotheses.text: The measures $\mu$ and $\nu$ are finite Borel measures on $\mathbb{R}^n$.
The vectors $X$ and $Y$ are measurable maps from one probability space to $\mathbb{R}^d$.
The factorization of the joint [characteristic function](c:characteristic-function) holds for every pair $(s,t)$.

conclusion: Equal characteristic functions give equal measures, and the factorization of the joint characteristic function holds if and only if $X$ and $Y$ are independent.

formal.difference: The declaration states the independence criterion of part (b). It does not state the uniqueness of part (a).

proofs.name: Gaussian smoothing
proofs.slogan: Smooth both measures with a Gaussian, recover them from their characteristic functions, then apply the uniqueness to the product law.
proofs.scope: Both parts. Part (a) is proved first, and part (b) uses it for the law of $(X,Y)$ in $\mathbb{R}^{2d}$.

roles.why: Finiteness makes the smoothed densities defined, and makes the dominated convergence step valid.
The two vectors have a joint law on $\mathbb{R}^{2d}$ that part (a) compares with the product law.
The factorization says that the joint law and the product law have equal characteristic functions.

steps.slogan: Compute the Gaussian characteristic function and write the Gaussian density as an integral of it.
steps.detail: The function $\varphi(t)=\int e^{itx}g(x)dx$ for the standard normal density $g$ satisfies $\varphi'=-t\varphi$ and $\varphi(0)=1$, so $\varphi(t)=e^{-t^2/2}$. Scaling and a product over coordinates give $g_\sigma(u)=(2\pi)^{-d}\int e^{i\langle t,u\rangle}e^{-\sigma^2|t|^2/2}dt$.

steps.slogan: Show that the Gaussian smoothing of a finite measure depends only on its characteristic function.
steps.detail: Let $h_\sigma(x)=\int g_\sigma(x-z)\,d\mu(z)$. Insert the formula for $g_\sigma$. The integrand is bounded by $e^{-\sigma^2|t|^2/2}$, so Fubini gives $h_\sigma(x)=(2\pi)^{-d}\int e^{i\langle t,x\rangle}e^{-\sigma^2|t|^2/2}\varphi_\mu(-t)\,dt$.

concepts.c:independent-random-variables: Independence is equivalent to a product law and to the factorization.

statement: Let $\xi_1,\xi_2,\dots$ be i.i.d. integrable variables with mean $\mu$. Put $S_n=\xi_1+\dots+\xi_n$. Let $T$ be a [stopping time](c:stopping-time) with $\mathbb{E}T<\infty$. Then $\mathbb{E}S_T=\mu\,\mathbb{E}T$. For the simple symmetric [random walk](c:random-walk) from $a\in\{0,\dots,N\}$ stopped at $0$ or $N$, $P(S_T=N)=a/N$ and $\mathbb{E}T=a(N-a)$.

hypotheses.text: The variables $\xi_i$ are i.i.d. with $\mathbb{E}|\xi_1|<\infty$ and mean $\mu$.
The time $T$ is a [stopping time](c:stopping-time) for $\mathcal{F}_n=\sigma(\xi_1,\dots,\xi_n)$, and $\mathbb{E}T<\infty$.
For the ruin problem, $\xi_i=\pm1$ with probability $1/2$ each, the [walk](c:random-walk) starts at $S_0=a$, and $T$ is the first time at $0$ or $N$.

conclusion: $\mathbb{E}S_T=\mu\,\mathbb{E}T$, and for the ruin problem $P(S_T=N)=a/N$ and $\mathbb{E}T=a(N-a)$.

formal.difference: The declaration states a criterion for submartingales through expected stopped values. It is related to optional stopping, but it is not Wald's identity.

proofs.name: Optional stopping and domination
proofs.slogan: Stop the martingale $S_n-n\mu$ at the bounded times $T\wedge n$, then let $n\to\infty$ by monotone and dominated convergence.
proofs.scope: The identity for every integrable i.i.d. sequence, and the two ruin formulas for the symmetric walk. The ruin case first proves $\mathbb{E}T<\infty$.

roles.why: Independence and equal means give $\mathbb{E}[\xi_{n+1}\mid\mathcal{F}_n]=\mu$, so $S_n-n\mu$ is a martingale.
The stopping time makes $T\wedge n$ a bounded stopping time, and $\mathbb{E}T<\infty$ supplies the integrable bound.
The $\pm1$ steps give mean $0$, bounded values $S_T\in\{0,N\}$, and the martingale $S_n^2-n$.

steps.slogan: Stop the [martingale](c:martingale) $S_n-n\mu$ at the bounded time $T\wedge n$.
steps.detail: The process $M_n=S_n-n\mu$ is a martingale, because $\mathbb{E}[\xi_{n+1}\mid\mathcal{F}_n]=\mu$. Bounded optional stopping at $0$ and $T\wedge n$ gives $\mathbb{E}M_{T\wedge n}=0$. So $\mathbb{E}S_{T\wedge n}=\mu\,\mathbb{E}[T\wedge n]$.

steps.slogan: Bound $|S_{T\wedge n}|$ by one integrable variable $Y$.
steps.detail: Let $Y=\sum_{i\le T}|\xi_i|$ and $m=\mathbb{E}|\xi_1|$. The last step for the variables $|\xi_i|$ gives $\mathbb{E}\sum_{i\le T\wedge n}|\xi_i|=m\,\mathbb{E}[T\wedge n]$. Monotone convergence gives $\mathbb{E}Y=m\,\mathbb{E}T<\infty$.

steps.slogan: Let $n\to\infty$ to get Wald's identity $\mathbb{E}S_T=\mu\,\mathbb{E}T$.
steps.detail: Since $T<\infty$ almost surely, $S_{T\wedge n}\to S_T$ almost surely, and $|S_{T\wedge n}|\le Y$. Dominated convergence gives $\mathbb{E}S_{T\wedge n}\to\mathbb{E}S_T$, and monotone convergence gives $\mathbb{E}[T\wedge n]\to\mathbb{E}T$.

steps.slogan: Show that the exit time of the symmetric walk has $\mathbb{E}T<\infty$.
steps.detail: After any block of $N$ steps, $N$ up-steps in a row take the walk to $N$, so the walk has left $\{1,\dots,N-1\}$. Hence $P(T>kN)\le(1-2^{-N})^k$. The tail sum $\sum_jP(T>j)$ is finite.

steps.slogan: Apply the identity with $\mu=0$ to get $P(S_T=N)=a/N$.
steps.detail: Apply Wald's identity to the walk $S_n-a$, which has mean $0$. It gives $\mathbb{E}S_T=a$. Since $S_T\in\{0,N\}$, $N\,P(S_T=N)=a$.

steps.slogan: Stop the martingale $S_n^2-n$ and let $n\to\infty$ to get $\mathbb{E}T=a(N-a)$.
steps.detail: The process $S_n^2-n$ is a martingale, because $\mathbb{E}[(S_n+\xi)^2\mid\mathcal{F}_n]=S_n^2+1$. Bounded optional stopping gives $\mathbb{E}S_{T\wedge n}^2=a^2+\mathbb{E}[T\wedge n]$. Since $S^2\le N^2$, dominated convergence gives $\mathbb{E}S_T^2=N^2\cdot a/N=aN$. So $\mathbb{E}T=aN-a^2$.

concepts.c:stopping-time: The stopping time is the random time at which the process is read.
concepts.c:martingale: A martingale has constant expectation, which stopping preserves.
concepts.c:random-walk: The gambler ruin problem is the exit problem of a symmetric walk.

statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $A$ an $m\times n$ matrix and $B$ an $n\times m$ matrix over $R$. For an $m$-element set $S\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}$, let $A_S$ hold the columns of $A$ in $S$ and $B_S$ the rows of $B$ in $S$. Then the [determinant](c:determinant) satisfies $\det(AB)=\sum_S\det(A_S)\det(B_S)$. If $n<m$, the sum is empty and $\det(AB)=0$.

hypotheses.text: The ring $R$ is commutative with $1$, and the proof uses no division.
The [matrix](c:matrix) $A$ is $m\times n$ and $B$ is $n\times m$, so $AB$ is square of size $m$.

conclusion: $\det(AB)=\sum_{|S|=m}\det(A_S)\det(B_S)$, and every $k\times k$ minor of $AB$ is the same sum over $k$-element sets $S$.

formal.difference: The declaration states that the exterior power is functorial for linear maps. That is the matrix identity for all minors in coordinate-free form.

proofs.name: Multilinear expansion of the columns
proofs.slogan: Expand each column of $AB$ in the columns of $A$, drop the maps that repeat a column, and group the rest by their image.
proofs.scope: All $m,n\ge0$. For $n<m$ no injective map exists, so the determinant is $0$.

roles.why: A commutative ring makes the determinant multilinear and alternating in the columns, with no division.
The shapes make $AB$ an $m\times m$ matrix whose column $j$ is $\sum_sB_{sj}a_s$.

steps.slogan: Expand each column of $AB$ in the columns of $A$ by multilinearity.
steps.detail: Column $j$ of $AB$ is $\sum_sB_{sj}a_s$. The [determinant](c:determinant) is multilinear in the columns, so $\det(AB)=\sum_f\big(\prod_jB_{f(j),j}\big)\det(a_{f(1)},\dots,a_{f(m)})$ over all maps $f\colon[m]\to[n]$.

steps.slogan: Drop the maps $f$ that are not injective, because they repeat a column.
steps.detail: If $f$ is not injective, two columns of the determinant are equal, so it is $0$. If $n<m$, no injective $f$ exists, and $\det(AB)=0$.

steps.slogan: Group the injective maps by their image $S$ and sort each image.
steps.detail: An injective $f$ with image $S=\{s_1<\dots<s_m\}$ has $f(j)=s_{\tau(j)}$ for a unique permutation $\tau$. Permuting the columns of $A_S$ multiplies its determinant by $\mathrm{sgn}(\tau)$. So $\det(AB)=\sum_S\det(A_S)\sum_\tau\mathrm{sgn}(\tau)\prod_jB_{s_{\tau(j)},j}$.

steps.slogan: Recognize the inner sum as the Leibniz formula for $\det(B_S)$.
steps.detail: The rows of $B_S$ are the rows $s_1,\dots,s_m$ of $B$. The term for $\tau$ is $\mathrm{sgn}(\tau)\prod_j(B_S)_{\tau(j),j}$. So the inner sum is $\det(B_S)$, and the first claim follows.

steps.slogan: Apply the result to the submatrices to get the formula for every minor.
steps.detail: The submatrix $(AB)_{I,J}$ equals $A_{I,[n]}B_{[n],J}$, a $k\times n$ matrix times an $n\times k$ matrix. The first claim gives $\det((AB)_{I,J})=\sum_{|S|=k}\det(A_{I,S})\det(B_{S,J})$. In matrix form, $C_k(AB)=C_k(A)C_k(B)$.

concepts.c:determinant: The determinant is multilinear and alternating in the columns, which drives the expansion.
concepts.c:matrix: The product $AB$ is a matrix whose columns are combinations of the columns of $A$.

statement: Let $K$ be a [number field](c:number-field) of degree $n$ with [ring of integers](c:ring-of-integers) $O_K$. For every nonzero $\alpha\in O_K$, the quotient $O_K/\alpha O_K$ by the [ideal](c:ideal) $\alpha O_K$ is finite of order $|N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)|$. So $\alpha$ is a unit if and only if $|N(\alpha)|=1$, and $\alpha$ is irreducible whenever $|N(\alpha)|$ is prime.

hypotheses.text: The field $K$ is a [number field](c:number-field), and $O_K$ is a free $\mathbb{Z}$-module of rank $n=[K:\mathbb{Q}]$.
The element $\alpha$ of the [ring of integers](c:ring-of-integers) $O_K$ is nonzero.
The norm $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)$ is the determinant of the $\mathbb{Q}$-linear map $x\mapsto\alpha x$ on $K$.

conclusion: The quotient $O_K/\alpha O_K$ is finite of order $|N(\alpha)|$ and isomorphic to $\bigoplus\mathbb{Z}/d_i$ for the invariant factors $d_i$ of the multiplication matrix, so unit and irreducibility criteria follow.

formal.difference: The declaration states that the absolute norm of the principal ideal $\alpha O_K$ equals $|N(\alpha)|$. It does not state the invariant factors or the unit and irreducibility criteria.

proofs.name: Multiplication matrix and Smith normal form
proofs.slogan: Write multiplication by $\alpha$ as an integer matrix, bring it to Smith normal form, and read the order of the quotient as its determinant.
proofs.scope: All nonzero $\alpha\in O_K$. The unit and irreducibility criteria follow from the order formula and the multiplicativity of the norm.

roles.why: A $\mathbb{Z}$-basis of $O_K$ identifies $O_K$ with $\mathbb{Z}^n$ and gives an integer matrix.
A nonzero $\alpha$ is invertible in $K$, so the matrix has nonzero determinant and the quotient is finite.
The definition of the norm as a determinant makes the determinant of the matrix equal to $N(\alpha)$.

steps.slogan: Write multiplication by $\alpha$ as an integer matrix $M_\alpha$ with $\det M_\alpha=N(\alpha)$.
steps.detail: Let $w_1,\dots,w_n$ be a $\mathbb{Z}$-basis of $O_K$. Then $\alpha w_j=\sum_i(M_\alpha)_{ij}w_i$ with integers, because $\alpha O_K\subseteq O_K$. The basis is also a $\mathbb{Q}$-basis of $K$, so $\det M_\alpha=N(\alpha)$.

steps.slogan: Identify the [ideal](c:ideal) $\alpha O_K$ with the lattice $M_\alpha\mathbb{Z}^n$.
steps.detail: Since $\alpha\ne0$ and $K$ is a field, $\det M_\alpha\ne0$, so $M_\alpha$ is injective. Under $O_K\cong\mathbb{Z}^n$, the image of multiplication by $\alpha$ is $\alpha O_K$. So $O_K/\alpha O_K\cong\mathbb{Z}^n/M_\alpha\mathbb{Z}^n$.

steps.slogan: Bring $M_\alpha$ to Smith normal form to read the order and the structure of the quotient.
steps.detail: There are invertible integer matrices $U$ and $V$ with $UM_\alpha V=\mathrm{diag}(d_1,\dots,d_n)$ and $d_1\mid\dots\mid d_n$. So the quotient is $\bigoplus\mathbb{Z}/d_i$ of order $\prod|d_i|=|\det M_\alpha|=|N(\alpha)|$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\alpha$ is a unit if and only if $|N(\alpha)|=1$.
steps.detail: An element $\alpha$ is a unit if and only if $\alpha O_K=O_K$. This holds if and only if the quotient has one element, so if and only if $|N(\alpha)|=1$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\alpha$ is irreducible when $|N(\alpha)|$ is prime.
steps.detail: If $|N(\alpha)|=p$ is prime, then $\alpha$ is not a unit. Let $\alpha=\beta\gamma$. The norm is multiplicative and has integer values on $O_K$, so $|N(\beta)||N(\gamma)|=p$. One factor has norm of absolute value $1$, so it is a unit.

concepts.c:ring-of-integers: The ring of integers is the free lattice that the matrix acts on.
concepts.c:ideal: The principal ideal is the image lattice, and the quotient by it is counted.

statement: Let $A$ be a real $n\times n$ matrix and let $P,Q$ be [positive definite](c:positive-definite-matrix) symmetric matrices with $A^TP+PA=-Q$. Let $g$ be continuous with $\|g(x)\|\le\kappa\|x\|$ for $\|x\|\le r$, and $2\kappa\lambda_{\max}(P)<\lambda_{\min}(Q)$. Then each solution of $x'=Ax+g(x)$ that starts in a small ball decays exponentially, so the origin is exponentially [stable](c:lyapunov-stability).

hypotheses.text: The matrices $P$ and $Q$ are symmetric and [positive definite](c:positive-definite-matrix), and $A^TP+PA=-Q$.
The map $g$ is continuous, and $\|g(x)\|\le\kappa\|x\|$ for $\|x\|\le r$.
The constants satisfy $2\kappa\lambda_{\max}(P)<\lambda_{\min}(Q)$.
The function $x$ is a $C^1$ solution of the [differential equation](c:ordinary-differential-equation) $x'=Ax+g(x)$ on $[0,T)$, with $\|x(0)\|<\rho$.

conclusion: With $c=(\lambda_{\min}(Q)-2\kappa\lambda_{\max}(P))/\lambda_{\max}(P)$ and $\rho=r\sqrt{\lambda_{\min}(P)/\lambda_{\max}(P)}$, every $t\in[0,T)$ has $\|x(t)\|\le r$, $x^TPx\le e^{-ct}x(0)^TPx(0)$, and $\|x(t)\|^2\le(\lambda_{\max}(P)/\lambda_{\min}(P))e^{-ct}\|x(0)\|^2$.

formal.difference: The declaration is a Grönwall bound for functions with a bounded derivative. It is a tool that the proof compares with, not this theorem.

proofs.name: Quadratic Lyapunov function
proofs.slogan: Differentiate $V=x^TPx$ along the solution, bound the derivative by $-cV$, and keep the solution inside the ball by continuity.
proofs.scope: All solutions with $\|x(0)\|<\rho$ on their interval $[0,T)$. The theorem does not assert that a solution exists.

roles.why: The symmetry of $P$ and $Q$ gives eigenvalue bounds on $V$, and the equation gives $\frac{d}{dt}V=-x^TQx+2x^TPg(x)$.
The bound on $g$ turns the cross term into at most $2\kappa\lambda_{\max}(P)\|x\|^2$ while the solution stays in the ball.
The inequality on the constants makes the coefficient $c$ of the decay positive.
The solution is $C^1$, so $V(x(t))$ is differentiable, and the start inside $\rho$ keeps it in the ball.

steps.slogan: Bound $V(x)=x^TPx$ above and below by multiples of $\|x\|^2$ with eigenvalues.
steps.detail: A symmetric matrix has an orthonormal eigenbasis, in which $x^TPx$ is a sum of eigenvalues times squared coordinates. So $\lambda_{\min}(P)\|x\|^2\le V(x)\le\lambda_{\max}(P)\|x\|^2$. The same holds for $Q$.

steps.slogan: Bound the derivative of $v(t)=V(x(t))$ by $-c\,v(t)$ while $\|x\|\le r$.
steps.detail: Symmetry of $P$ gives $v'=x^T(A^TP+PA)x+2x^TPg(x)=-x^TQx+2x^TPg(x)$. Here $x^TQx\ge\lambda_{\min}(Q)\|x\|^2$ and $|x^TPg(x)|\le\lambda_{\max}(P)\kappa\|x\|^2$. Since $\|x\|^2\ge v/\lambda_{\max}(P)$, we get $v'\le-cv$. This quadratic [Lyapunov function](c:lyapunov-function) decreases along the solution.

steps.slogan: Integrate the differential inequality to get $v(t)\le v(0)e^{-ct}$.
steps.detail: The function $w=ve^{ct}$ has $w'=(v'+cv)e^{ct}\le0$, so $w$ does not increase. This is the Grönwall comparison with the rate $-c$.

steps.slogan: Keep the solution inside the ball by a continuity argument.
steps.detail: Let $S$ be the set of $s$ with $\|x\|\le r$ on $[0,s]$. It contains $0$. On $S$, $\|x(s)\|^2\le v(0)/\lambda_{\min}(P)<r^2$, so $\|x\|<r$ strictly. If $s^*=\sup S<T$, continuity keeps $\|x\|\le r$ just after $s^*$, which contradicts the choice of $s^*$. So $S=[0,T)$.

steps.slogan: Convert the decay of $v$ into the three stated bounds and into stability.
steps.detail: Use the norm bounds twice: $\|x(t)\|^2\le v(t)/\lambda_{\min}(P)\le e^{-ct}\lambda_{\max}(P)\|x(0)\|^2/\lambda_{\min}(P)$. For $\varepsilon>0$, choose $\delta=\min(\rho,\varepsilon\sqrt{\lambda_{\min}(P)/\lambda_{\max}(P)})$. Then $\|x(0)\|<\delta$ gives $\|x(t)\|<\varepsilon$ for all $t$ and $\|x(t)\|\to0$, which is [Lyapunov stability](c:lyapunov-stability) with decay.

concepts.c:positive-definite-matrix: Positive definite $P$ and $Q$ give the eigenvalue bounds that compare $V$ with the norm.
concepts.c:lyapunov-stability: The decay bound proves that small starts stay small and tend to the origin.
concepts.c:ordinary-differential-equation: The solution of this equation is the curve that the Lyapunov function follows.
concepts.c:lyapunov-function: The quadratic function $V$ falls along every solution inside the ball.

statement: Apply a one-step method to $y'=\lambda y$ to get $y_{n+1}=R(z)y_n$ with $z=h\lambda$. Then $y_n=R(z)^ny_0$, so $y_n\to0$ if $|R(z)|<1$ and $|y_n|\to\infty$ if $|R(z)|>1$ and $y_0\ne0$. For an explicit [Runge-Kutta method](c:runge-kutta-method), $R$ is a nonconstant [polynomial](c:polynomial), so $\{|R|<1\}$ does not contain the half plane $\operatorname{Re}z<0$.

hypotheses.text: The [initial value problem](c:initial-value-problem) is the linear test equation $y'=\lambda y$ with $\lambda\in\mathbb{C}$, and the method gives $y_{n+1}=R(z)y_n$.
The stage equations of an implicit method have a unique solution; for backward Euler $z\ne1$, and for the trapezoidal rule $z\ne2$.
For the last claim, the method is an explicit [Runge-Kutta method](c:runge-kutta-method) with $\sum b_i=1$.

conclusion: The powers $R(z)^n$ govern decay and growth; $R$ is $1+z$, $1/(1-z)$ and $(1+z/2)/(1-z/2)$ for explicit Euler, backward Euler and the trapezoidal rule, with stability sets the disc $|z+1|<1$, a set containing $\operatorname{Re}z<0$, and exactly $\operatorname{Re}z<0$.

formal.difference: The declaration is a neighbouring mathlib fact. It states a related or smaller result in the form that mathlib uses.

proofs.name: Stability function
proofs.slogan: Compute the stability function of each method, read decay from its powers, and show that a polynomial cannot be stable on the whole half plane.
proofs.scope: The three listed methods and every explicit Runge-Kutta method with $\sum b_i=1$. The set $\{|R|\le1\}$ is not studied.

roles.why: On the test equation each step multiplies by the same number $R(z)$, so the solution is a geometric sequence.
The conditions on $z$ let the implicit stage equations be solved, so $R$ is defined.
The Runge-Kutta form makes $R$ a polynomial with $R'(0)=\sum b_i=1$, which is not constant.

steps.slogan: Prove by induction that $y_n=R(z)^ny_0$ and read decay or growth from $|R(z)|$.
steps.detail: Each step multiplies by the same $R(z)$, so $y_n=R(z)^ny_0$. If $|R(z)|<1$, then $|y_n|=|R|^n|y_0|\to0$. If $|R(z)|>1$ and $y_0\ne0$, then $|y_n|\to\infty$.

steps.slogan: Compute $R$ for explicit Euler and backward Euler and find their stability sets.
steps.detail: Explicit Euler gives $R=1+z$, and $|R|<1$ is the open disc of radius $1$ about $-1$. Backward Euler gives $R=1/(1-z)$. For $z=x+iy$ with $x<0$, $|1-z|^2\ge(1-x)^2>1$, so $|R|<1$ on the left half plane.

steps.slogan: Compute $R$ for the trapezoidal rule and show that its set is exactly $\operatorname{Re}z<0$.
steps.detail: The rule gives $R=(1+z/2)/(1-z/2)$. For $z=x+iy$, $|1+z/2|^2-|1-z/2|^2=2x$. So $|R(z)|<1$ if and only if $x<0$.

steps.slogan: Show by induction on the stages that $R$ is a nonconstant polynomial.
steps.detail: On the test equation, $Y_i=y_n+z\sum_{j<i}a_{ij}Y_j$. By induction, $Y_i=P_i(z)y_n$ with polynomials $P_i$ and $P_i(0)=1$. Then $R(z)=1+z\sum b_iP_i(z)$ is a polynomial with $R'(0)=\sum b_i=1$.

steps.slogan: Find a point of the left half plane where the polynomial $R$ has $|R|>1$.
steps.detail: Let $R$ have degree $d\ge1$. The real polynomial $q(t)=|R(-t)|^2$ has degree $2d$ and a positive leading coefficient, so $q(t)\to\infty$. Hence $q(t_0)>1$ for some $t_0>0$, and $z=-t_0$ lies outside the region.

steps.slogan: Collect the three parts into the stated theorem.
steps.detail: Part (i) is the first step, part (ii) holds by the steps for the three methods, and part (iii) holds because the polynomial has a point outside the region in the left half plane.

concepts.c:initial-value-problem: The test equation is the initial value problem on which the stability function is defined.
concepts.c:runge-kutta-method: Explicit Runge-Kutta methods give stability functions that are polynomials.
concepts.c:polynomial: A nonconstant polynomial grows without bound along a real ray.

statement: A finite [projective plane](c:projective-plane) has finitely many points and lines with an incidence relation. Two distinct points lie on exactly one line. Two distinct lines meet in exactly one point. Four points exist, no three on a line. Then some integer $n\ge2$ makes every line hold $n+1$ points, every point lie on $n+1$ lines, and the plane have $n^2+n+1$ points and $n^2+n+1$ lines.

hypotheses.text: The sets of points and lines are [finite](c:finite-set), and a line is identified with its set of points.
Two distinct points lie on exactly one line (A1), two distinct lines meet in exactly one point (A2), and four points exist with no three on a line (A3).

conclusion: There is an integer $n\ge2$ such that every line has $n+1$ points, every point is on $n+1$ lines, and there are $n^2+n+1$ points and $n^2+n+1$ lines.

formal.difference: The declaration is a neighbouring mathlib fact. It states a related or smaller result in the form that mathlib uses.

proofs.name: Counting points and lines through a point
proofs.slogan: Match the points of a line with the lines through an outside point, show that all lines have equal size, then count.
proofs.scope: All finite planes with the three axioms. The proof first finds, for two lines, a point on neither.

roles.why: Finiteness makes the common size of the lines an integer and makes the final counts finite sums.
The axioms give the line through two points, the meeting point of two lines, and the four-point configuration.

steps.slogan: Match the points of a line $\ell$ with the lines through a point $P$ off $\ell$.
steps.detail: Send a point $Q$ on $\ell$ to the line $PQ$, which is unique by (A1). If $PQ=PQ'$ for $Q\ne Q'$, that line shares two points with $\ell$, so it equals $\ell$ by (A2). This is false, because $P$ is not on $\ell$. A line $m$ through $P$ meets $\ell$ in one point $Q$ by (A2), so $m=PQ$. Hence the map is a bijection.

steps.slogan: Show that for any two lines some point lies on neither line.
steps.detail: Let the lines $\ell\ne m$ meet at $X$, and suppose that every point is on one of them. The four points of (A3) then split two and two between $\ell$ and $m$, all different from $X$. The lines $ac$ and $bd$ meet at a point $Y$ on $\ell$ or $m$. Each case contradicts (A2) or (A3).

steps.slogan: Show that all lines have the same number $n+1$ of points, as does the number of lines at a point.
steps.detail: For lines $\ell$ and $m$, pick $P$ on neither. By the bijection, $|\ell|$ and $|m|$ both equal the number of lines through $P$. So all lines have $n+1$ points. Every point lies off some line, so every point is on $n+1$ lines.

steps.slogan: Show that $n\ge2$ by finding three points on one line.
steps.detail: With the four points $a,b,c,d$ of (A3), the lines $ab$ and $cd$ meet at a point $Z$ by (A2). The point $Z$ is not $a$ or $b$, since three of the four points would then be collinear. So the line $ab$ holds $a$, $b$ and $Z$, and $n+1\ge3$.

steps.slogan: Count the points and the lines through one point and one line.
steps.detail: Fix a point $P$. Each other point is on exactly one line through $P$, there are $n+1$ such lines, and each has $n$ other points. So there are $1+(n+1)n=n^2+n+1$ points. Dually, a line $\ell$ has $n+1$ points, and each is on $n$ other lines, so there are $n^2+n+1$ lines.

concepts.c:projective-plane: The axioms define the plane whose point and line counts the theorem gives.
concepts.c:finite-set: Finite sets make every count an integer.

statement: Let $G$ be a finite simple [graph](c:graph) with $n\ge1$ vertices and complement $G^c$. Write $\chi=\chi(G)$ and $\chi^c=\chi(G^c)$ for the [chromatic numbers](c:chromatic-number). Then $\chi\chi^c\ge n$, $\chi+\chi^c\le n+1$ and $\chi\chi^c\le((n+1)/2)^2$. So $\chi+\chi^c\ge2\sqrt n$.

hypotheses.text: The [graph](c:graph) $G$ is finite and simple.
The complement $G^c$ has the same vertices, and two distinct vertices are adjacent in $G^c$ if and only if they are not adjacent in $G$.
The chromatic number is the least number of colors in a proper [coloring](c:graph-coloring).

conclusion: The bounds $n\le\chi\chi^c\le((n+1)/2)^2$ and $2\sqrt n\le\chi+\chi^c\le n+1$ hold.

formal.difference: The declaration states that a graph with a proper $k$-coloring has chromatic number at most $k$. It is a tool for the upper bounds, not the theorem.

proofs.name: Pair map and induction on vertices
proofs.slogan: Map each vertex to its pair of colors for the lower bound, remove a vertex for the upper bound, and use the AM-GM inequality.
proofs.scope: All finite simple graphs. The sum bound is proved by induction on $n$, with a case split on whether a vertex raises a chromatic number.

roles.why: A finite graph has a vertex to remove and a finite chromatic number, which supports the induction.
Every pair of distinct vertices is an edge of $G$ or of $G^c$, which makes the pair map injective and splits degrees as $d$ and $n-1-d$.
Proper colorings give color classes that are independent, and they give the bounds $\chi(G)\le\chi(H)+1$.

steps.slogan: Map each vertex to its pair of colors to show $n\le\chi\chi^c$.
steps.detail: Take proper colorings $c$ of $G$ and $c'$ of $G^c$, and set $\Phi(v)=(c(v),c'(v))$. If $\Phi(u)=\Phi(v)$ for $u\ne v$, then $u,v$ are non-adjacent in both $G$ and $G^c$. That is false, so $\Phi$ is injective. Hence $n\le\chi\chi^c$.

steps.slogan: Remove a vertex $v$ and bound both chromatic numbers by one more than those of $H=G-v$.
steps.detail: Use induction on $n$. For $n=1$, $\chi+\chi^c=2=n+1$. For $n\ge2$ let $H=G-v$, so $H^c=G^c-v$. A new color for $v$ gives $\chi\le\chi(H)+1$ and $\chi^c\le\chi(H^c)+1$.

steps.slogan: Handle the case where one of the two inequalities is strict.
steps.detail: Then $\chi+\chi^c\le\chi(H)+\chi(H^c)+1$, because only one of the two numbers grows by one. By the induction hypothesis this is at most $(n-1+1)+1=n+1$.

steps.slogan: Handle the case with equality in both by comparing degrees with colors.
steps.detail: If $\chi=\chi(H)+1$, then $\deg_G(v)\ge\chi(H)$; otherwise the neighbors of $v$ miss a color and $\chi\le\chi(H)$. Likewise $n-1-\deg_G(v)\ge\chi(H^c)$. Adding gives $n-1\ge\chi(H)+\chi(H^c)$, so $\chi+\chi^c\le n+1$.

steps.slogan: Apply the AM-GM inequality to the bounds to get the sum and product estimates.
steps.detail: The inequality $\chi+\chi^c\ge2\sqrt{\chi\chi^c}\ge2\sqrt n$ gives the lower bound for the sum. The inequality $\chi\chi^c\le((\chi+\chi^c)/2)^2\le((n+1)/2)^2$ gives the upper bound for the product.

concepts.c:chromatic-number: The chromatic numbers are the quantities that the theorem bounds.
concepts.c:graph-coloring: Proper colorings define the pair map and the new color for a removed vertex.

statement: Let $V\ne0$ be a finite-dimensional space over a field. Let $L\subseteq\mathfrak{gl}(V)$ be a Lie subalgebra of [nilpotent](c:nilpotent-endomorphism) endomorphisms. Then some $v\ne0$ has $xv=0$ for all $x\in L$, and $V$ has a basis making $L$ strictly upper triangular. A finite-dimensional Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ is [nilpotent](c:nilpotent-lie-algebra) if and only if every $\operatorname{ad}(x)$ is nilpotent.

hypotheses.text: The field $F$ is arbitrary, and no assumption on the characteristic is needed.
The space $V$ is finite-dimensional and nonzero.
The bracket on $L$ is the commutator $[x,y]=xy-yx$.
For the last claim, $\mathfrak g$ is a finite-dimensional Lie algebra, and $\operatorname{ad}(x)$ is the [adjoint](c:adjoint-representation) map.

conclusion: There is a common kernel vector, a basis with $L$ strictly upper triangular, and a vanishing product of $\dim V$ elements of $L$. A Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ is nilpotent if and only if every $\operatorname{ad}(x)$ is nilpotent.

formal.difference: The declaration states that a Noetherian Lie module is Engelian, in the form that mathlib uses. It is a related fact, and it does not state the flag and the criterion.

proofs.name: Induction with a maximal proper subalgebra
proofs.slogan: Take a maximal proper subalgebra, show that it is an ideal of codimension one, and find a common kernel vector in the fixed space of the ideal.
proofs.scope: The full statement. The common kernel vector is proved by induction on $\dim L$, the flag by induction on $\dim V$, and the criterion by the flag.

roles.why: No division by the characteristic is used, since the proof only uses commutators and a binomial formula for commuting maps.
A nonzero finite-dimensional space gives a nonzero quotient and makes the induction on dimension end.
The commutator bracket gives $\operatorname{ad}(x)=\lambda_x-\rho_x$ on $\operatorname{End}(V)$ and $x(zw)=z(xw)+[x,z]w$.
The adjoint map turns a statement on the Lie algebra into a statement on nilpotent operators.

steps.slogan: Show that $\operatorname{ad}(x)$ is a nilpotent operator on the quotient $L/K$ for $x\in K$.
steps.detail: Let $K$ be a maximal proper subalgebra of $L$. The left and right multiplications $\lambda_x,\rho_x$ commute and are nilpotent, so $\operatorname{ad}(x)=\lambda_x-\rho_x$ is nilpotent by the binomial formula. It preserves $K$, so it acts as a nilpotent map on $L/K\ne0$.

steps.slogan: Use induction to show that $K$ is an ideal of $L$ with $\dim L/K=1$.
steps.detail: The image of $K$ in $\mathfrak{gl}(L/K)$ has smaller dimension than $L$, so induction gives $y\notin K$ with $[K,y]\subseteq K$. The normalizer of $K$ is a subalgebra that contains $K$ strictly, so it equals $L$. Any line in $L/K$ lifts to a subalgebra, so $L=K+Fz$.

steps.slogan: Find a nonzero common kernel vector of $L$ inside the fixed space $W$ of $K$.
steps.detail: Induction on $\dim L$ shows that $W=\{v:Kv=0\}$ is nonzero. Since $x(zw)=z(xw)+[x,z]w=0$, $zW\subseteq W$. The nilpotent map $z$ has a nonzero kernel vector $w\in W$, and then $Lw=0$.

steps.slogan: Pass to $V/V_1$ and lift a basis to make $L$ strictly upper triangular.
steps.detail: Let $V_1$ be the space of common kernel vectors. By induction on $\dim V$, $L$ is strictly upper triangular on $V/V_1$. Put a basis of $V_1$ in front of the lifted basis. A product of $\dim V$ strictly upper triangular matrices is $0$.

steps.slogan: Prove the criterion for $\mathfrak g$ from the flag in the adjoint representation.
steps.detail: If $C^k\mathfrak g=0$, then $\operatorname{ad}(x)^{k-1}y\in C^k\mathfrak g=0$, so $\operatorname{ad}(x)$ is nilpotent. Conversely, $\operatorname{ad}(\mathfrak g)$ consists of nilpotent maps, so a product of $n=\dim\mathfrak g$ of them is $0$. Hence $C^{n+1}\mathfrak g=0$ and $\mathfrak g$ is nilpotent.

concepts.c:nilpotent-endomorphism: A nilpotent map has a nonzero kernel vector, which drives the proof.
concepts.c:nilpotent-lie-algebra: The criterion says when the lower central series ends at zero.
concepts.c:adjoint-representation: The adjoint map turns brackets into operators that can be nilpotent.

statement: Let $f,g\in R[y]$ with $\deg f\le m$, $\deg g\le n$ and $m+n\ge1$. Let $\operatorname{Res}$ be the [resultant](c:resultant), the Sylvester determinant. Then $fp+gq=\operatorname{Res}$ for some $p,q$ with $\deg p<n$ and $\deg q<m$. Over a field, with exact degrees, $\operatorname{Res}=0$ if and only if $f,g$ have a common factor of positive degree.

hypotheses.text: The ring $R$ is commutative, and the [polynomials](c:polynomial-ring) are in one variable $y$.
In part (a), $\deg f\le m$, $\deg g\le n$ and $m+n\ge1$.
In part (b), the base is a field, $f,g$ are nonzero, and the degrees are exactly $m$ and $n$.
In part (c), the leading coefficients in $y$ do not vanish at the chosen point.

conclusion: There are $p,q$ with $fp+gq=\operatorname{Res}_{m,n}(f,g)$, the resultant vanishes over a field if and only if there is a common factor, and in part (c) it vanishes at $a$ if and only if the specialized polynomials have a common root.

proofs.name: Sylvester map and adjugate
proofs.slogan: Write the pair map as a square matrix, solve for the constant polynomial with the adjugate, and read common factors from its kernel.
proofs.scope: Parts (a), (b) and (c), and the elimination statement that a common zero of $f$ and $g$ kills the resultant.

roles.why: A commutative ring has an adjugate with $M\operatorname{adj}(M)=\det(M)I$.
The degree bounds make $(p,q)\mapsto fp+gq$ a square matrix $M$ of size $m+n$.
A field gives kernels for singular matrices, and $K[y]$ has no zero divisors and unique factors.
Nonzero leading coefficients keep the degrees exact after specialization.

steps.detail: The determinant commutes with ring homomorphisms. So the resultant of $f(a,y),g(a,y)$ with formal degrees $m,n$ is $\operatorname{Res}_y(f,g)(a)$. The degrees stay exact, so part (b) over the closure $\bar K$ gives a common root exactly when it vanishes.

steps.slogan: Evaluate the Bezout identity at a common zero to get elimination.
steps.detail: Apply part (a) with $R=A$ to get $fp+gq=\operatorname{Res}_y(f,g)\in A$. At a common zero $(a,b)$ the left side is $0\cdot p(a,b)+0\cdot q(a,b)=0$. So $\operatorname{Res}_y(f,g)(a)=0$.

statement: Let $0\to M'\xrightarrow{f}M\xrightarrow{g}M''\to0$ be a short [exact sequence](c:exact-sequence) of $R$-modules. Then $M$ is [Noetherian](c:noetherian-module) if and only if $M'$ and $M''$ are Noetherian. If $R$ is a [Noetherian ring](c:noetherian-ring), every finitely generated $R$-module is Noetherian. A module is Noetherian when every ascending chain of submodules becomes constant.

hypotheses.text: The map $f$ is injective, $g$ is surjective, and $\operatorname{im}f=\ker g$.
For part (b), $R$ is a left Noetherian ring, and the modules are left modules.
A ring is Noetherian when it is Noetherian as a module over itself.

conclusion: The module $M$ is Noetherian if and only if $M'$ and $M''$ are, and for a Noetherian ring every finitely generated module is Noetherian.

formal.difference: The declaration is a neighbouring mathlib fact. It states a related or smaller result in the form that mathlib uses.

proofs.name: Pull chains back along the sequence
proofs.slogan: Split a chain in $M$ into chains in $M'$ and $M''$, lift their stopping back to $M$, and reach finite generation through free modules.
proofs.scope: Part (a) in both directions, and part (b) by induction on free modules followed by a surjection from a free module.

roles.why: Exactness gives $\ker g=\operatorname{im}f$, which lifts equality of images and preimages to equality of submodules.
Part (b) uses the left module structure on $R^n$ and the sequences $0\to R^{n-1}\to R^n\to R\to0$.
The ring $R$ is Noetherian as a module over itself, which is the base case for $R^n$.

steps.slogan: If $M$ is Noetherian, show that $M'$ and $M''$ are Noetherian.
steps.detail: A chain in $M'$ maps by the injective map $f$ to a chain in $M$, which stops, so the chain in $M'$ stops. A chain $N_k$ in $M''$ gives the chain $g^{-1}(N_k)$ in $M$, and $g(g^{-1}(N_k))=N_k$ since $g$ is onto.

steps.slogan: Given a chain $N_k$ in $M$, take its images and preimages in the end modules.
steps.detail: The chains $f^{-1}(N_k)$ in $M'$ and $g(N_k)$ in $M''$ ascend. Both are constant from some index $K$ on, since $M'$ and $M''$ are Noetherian.

steps.slogan: Show that $N_k=N_{k+1}$ for $k\ge K$ by lifting through the sequence.
steps.detail: Take $x\in N_{k+1}$. Then $g(x)=g(y)$ for some $y\in N_k$, so $x-y\in\ker g=\operatorname{im}f$. Write $x-y=f(z)$. Then $z\in f^{-1}(N_{k+1})=f^{-1}(N_k)$, so $x-y\in N_k$ and $x\in N_k$.

steps.slogan: Prove by induction on $n$ that the free module $R^n$ is Noetherian.
steps.detail: The module $R^0$ is zero. For $n\ge1$ use the exact sequence $0\to R^{n-1}\to R^n\to R\to0$ that drops the last coordinate. The ends are Noetherian, so $R^n$ is Noetherian by part (a).

steps.slogan: Write a finitely generated module as a quotient of $R^n$.
steps.detail: If $M$ has $n$ generators, there is a surjection $R^n\to M$ with kernel $K$. The sequence $0\to K\to R^n\to M\to0$ is exact. Since $R^n$ is Noetherian, part (a) forward shows that $M$ is Noetherian.

concepts.c:exact-sequence: Exactness ties kernel and image and lets chains move across the sequence.
concepts.c:noetherian-module: The chain condition on submodules is what the theorem transfers.
concepts.c:noetherian-ring: A Noetherian ring gives the base case for free modules.

statement: Let $f\in C^{n+1}[a,b]$, let $x_0,\dots,x_n$ be distinct nodes, let $p$ be the [interpolating](c:polynomial-approximation) [polynomial](c:polynomial) of degree at most $n$, and $\omega(t)=\prod(t-x_i)$. Then $f(x)-p(x)=f^{(n+1)}(\xi)\omega(x)/(n+1)!$ for some $\xi$ in the hull of $x$ and the nodes. On $[-1,1]$, $\max|\omega|\ge2^{-n}$, with equality for Chebyshev nodes.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is $n+1$ times continuously differentiable on $[a,b]$, and the nodes are pairwise distinct.
The last claim uses the interval $[-1,1]$. For $[a,b]$ an affine change of variable gives $\max|\omega|\ge2((b-a)/4)^{n+1}$.

conclusion: The error is $f^{(n+1)}(\xi)\omega(x)/(n+1)!$, so $\max|f-p|\le\frac{M}{(n+1)!}\max|\omega|$, and Chebyshev nodes give the bound $M/(2^n(n+1)!)$ on $[-1,1]$.

formal.difference: The declaration states that a polynomial of small degree equals its Lagrange interpolant on the nodes. It covers existence and uniqueness, not the error formula.

proofs.name: Repeated Rolle theorem
proofs.slogan: Subtract a multiple of $\omega$ so that the error function has $n+2$ zeros, then apply Rolle's theorem $n+1$ times to find $\xi$.
proofs.scope: The identity at nodes and non-nodes, the error bound, the optimal nodes on $[-1,1]$ and the case of a general interval.

roles.why: The $C^{n+1}$ condition lets Rolle's theorem apply to each derivative up to order $n$ and gives the final derivative.
On $[-1,1]$ the minimax property of monic polynomials fixes the best nodes, and an affine map moves them to $[a,b]$.

steps.slogan: Show that the interpolating polynomial $p$ exists and is unique.
steps.detail: The Vandermonde matrix of $n+1$ distinct nodes is invertible, so exactly one polynomial of degree at most $n$ takes the given values. The Lagrange sum $\sum f(x_i)\ell_i$ is of degree at most $n$ and has these values.

steps.slogan: Build $g=f-p-c\,\omega$ with $n+2$ distinct zeros.
steps.detail: For a non-node $x$ we have $\omega(x)\ne0$. Put $c=(f(x)-p(x))/\omega(x)$ and $g(t)=f(t)-p(t)-c\,\omega(t)$. Then $g$ is $C^{n+1}$ and vanishes at all nodes and at $x$. For a node, the identity holds with $\xi=x$.

steps.slogan: Apply Rolle's theorem repeatedly to find a zero of $g^{(n+1)}$.
steps.detail: Between two consecutive zeros of $g$ lies a zero of $g'$. By induction, $g^{(j)}$ has at least $n+2-j$ distinct zeros in the open hull. For $j=n+1$ we get a zero $\xi$ of $g^{(n+1)}$.

steps.slogan: Compute $g^{(n+1)}$ and read off the error formula and the bound.
steps.detail: We have $p^{(n+1)}=0$ and $\omega^{(n+1)}=(n+1)!$, so $g^{(n+1)}=f^{(n+1)}-c\,(n+1)!$. At $\xi$ this is $0$, so $f(x)-p(x)=f^{(n+1)}(\xi)\omega(x)/(n+1)!$. If $|f^{(n+1)}|\le M$, take absolute values.

steps.slogan: Choose the nodes by the Chebyshev minimax theorem and rescale to $[a,b]$.
steps.detail: The polynomial $\omega$ is monic of degree $n+1$. On $[-1,1]$, $\max|\omega|\ge2^{-n}$, with equality if and only if $\omega=2^{-n}T_{n+1}$, so the nodes are the zeros of $T_{n+1}$. The affine map to $[a,b]$ gives $2((b-a)/4)^{n+1}$.

concepts.c:polynomial-approximation: The interpolating polynomial is the approximation whose error is measured.
concepts.c:polynomial: The node polynomial and the interpolant are polynomials of known degree.

statement: Let $A$ be an invertible real [matrix](c:matrix), $\|\cdot\|$ the operator [norm](c:norm), and $\kappa(A)=\|A\|\|A^{-1}\|$ the [condition number](c:condition-number). If $Ax=b\ne0$ and $A(x+\delta x)=b+\delta b$, then $\|\delta x\|/\|x\|\le\kappa(A)\|\delta b\|/\|b\|$. If $\kappa(A)\varepsilon<1$ for $\varepsilon=\|\delta A\|/\|A\|$, then $A+\delta A$ is invertible and the relative error is at most $\kappa\varepsilon/(1-\kappa\varepsilon)$.

hypotheses.text: The matrix $A$ is invertible and $b\ne0$.
In part (b), $\kappa(A)\|\delta A\|/\|A\|<1$.
Parts (c) and (d) use the Euclidean norm and the singular values of $A$.

conclusion: Part (a) bounds the relative error by $\kappa(A)\|\delta b\|/\|b\|$, part (b) by $\kappa\varepsilon/(1-\kappa\varepsilon)$, part (c) is sharp, and part (d) says the distance to a singular matrix is $1/\kappa_2=\sigma_{\min}/\sigma_{\max}$.

formal.difference: The declaration states that $1-x$ has an inverse given by the Neumann series for small $x$ in a normed ring. It is the tool for part (b), not the whole theorem.

proofs.name: Neumann series and singular vectors
proofs.slogan: Subtract the two systems for the bounds, use the Neumann series to invert the perturbed matrix, and test sharpness on singular vectors.
proofs.scope: Parts (a) to (d), with the Euclidean norm for the sharpness and distance claims.

roles.why: Invertibility lets us write $\delta x=A^{-1}\delta b$, and $b\ne0$ lets us divide by $\|b\|$.
The smallness of $\kappa\varepsilon$ makes the Neumann series converge.
The singular value decomposition gives $\|A\|_2=\sigma_1$ and $\|A^{-1}\|_2=1/\sigma_n$, with explicit vectors.

steps.slogan: Bound the error from a change in $b$ by $\|A^{-1}\|\|\delta b\|$ and divide by $\|x\|$.
steps.detail: Subtracting $Ax=b$ gives $A\delta x=\delta b$, so $\|\delta x\|\le\|A^{-1}\|\|\delta b\|$. Since $\|b\|\le\|A\|\|x\|$, we get $\|\delta x\|/\|x\|\le\kappa(A)\|\delta b\|/\|b\|$.

steps.slogan: Write $A+\delta A=A(I+B)$ and invert it with the Neumann series.
steps.detail: With $B=A^{-1}\delta A$ we have $\|B\|\le\kappa\varepsilon<1$. The Neumann series shows that $I+B$ is invertible with $\|(I+B)^{-1}\|\le1/(1-\|B\|)$. So $\|(A+\delta A)^{-1}\|\le\|A^{-1}\|/(1-\kappa\varepsilon)$.

steps.slogan: Bound the error from a change in $A$ using the inverse bound.
steps.detail: Subtracting $Ax=b$ from $(A+\delta A)(x+\delta x)=b$ gives $(A+\delta A)\delta x=-\delta A\,x$. So $\|\delta x\|\le\|A^{-1}\|\|\delta A\|\|x\|/(1-\kappa\varepsilon)$. Divide by $\|x\|$ to get $\kappa\varepsilon/(1-\kappa\varepsilon)$.

steps.slogan: Use singular vectors to show that part (a) is sharp for the Euclidean norm.
steps.detail: Write $Av_i=\sigma_iu_i$ with $\sigma_1\ge\dots\ge\sigma_n>0$, so $\kappa_2=\sigma_1/\sigma_n$. Take $x=v_1$, $b=\sigma_1u_1$ and $\delta b=tu_n$. Then $\delta x=tv_n/\sigma_n$, and the ratio of relative errors is $\sigma_1/\sigma_n$.

steps.slogan: Show that the relative distance to a singular matrix is exactly $1/\kappa_2$.
steps.detail: If $\|\delta A\|_2<\sigma_n$, then $\|A^{-1}\delta A\|<1$, so $A+\delta A$ is invertible. For $\delta A=-\sigma_nu_nv_n^T$ we have $\|\delta A\|_2=\sigma_n$ and $(A+\delta A)v_n=0$. So the least relative size is $\sigma_n/\sigma_1$.

concepts.c:matrix: The perturbed system is a matrix equation that we invert.
concepts.c:norm: The operator norm bounds products and inverses of the matrices.
concepts.c:condition-number: The condition number is the factor that magnifies relative errors.
