statement: Let $H(p)=-p\log_2p-(1-p)\log_2(1-p)$ be the binary [entropy](c:entropy). For integers $0<k\le n/2$, $\sum_{j\le k}\binom nj\le2^{nH(k/n)}$ and $\binom nk\ge2^{nH(k/n)}/(n+1)$. For a [binomial](c:binomial-distribution) variable $X$ with $n$ trials and probability $1/2$, $P(X\le k)\le2^{-n(1-H(k/n))}$.

hypotheses.text: The numbers $n$ and $k$ are integers with $0<k\le n/2$.
The entropy is evaluated at the rational point $p=k/n$.

conclusion: The sum of [binomial coefficients](c:binomial-coefficient) up to $k$ is at most $2^{nH(k/n)}$, the coefficient $\binom nk$ is at least $2^{nH(k/n)}/(n+1)$, and the tail bound holds.

formal.difference: The declaration rewrites binary entropy as a sum of two $-x\log x$ terms. It is a related fact about the function $H$, not the bounds.

proofs.name: Binomial expansion at the point k/n
proofs.slogan: Expand $1=(p+q)^n$, compare each term with the term at $j=k$, and bound the largest term from below.
proofs.scope: The upper bound on the sum, the lower bound on one coefficient, and the tail bound, for $0<k\le n/2$.

roles.why: The condition $0<k\le n/2$ gives $p\le q$ and $0<k/n<1$.
At $p=k/n$ the term $p^kq^{n-k}$ equals $2^{-nH(p)}$.

steps.slogan: Expand $1=(p+q)^n$ with $p=k/n$ and $q=1-p$ by the binomial theorem.
steps.detail: Then $1=\sum_{j=0}^n\binom njp^jq^{n-j}$, and every term is nonnegative. Let $t_j$ be the $j$-th term.

steps.slogan: For $j\le k$ show that $p^jq^{n-j}\ge p^kq^{n-k}$.
steps.detail: Since $p\le1/2$, we have $p\le q$. So $p^jq^{n-j}=p^kq^{n-k}(q/p)^{k-j}\ge p^kq^{n-k}$ for $j\le k$.

steps.slogan: Get the upper bound on the sum from the first two steps.
steps.detail: We have $1\ge\sum_{j\le k}t_j\ge p^kq^{n-k}\sum_{j\le k}\binom nj$. Also $\log_2(p^kq^{n-k})=-nH(p)$. So $\sum_{j\le k}\binom nj\le2^{nH(p)}$.

steps.slogan: Show that the term $t_j$ is largest at $j=k$.
steps.detail: The ratio is $t_{j+1}/t_j=(n-j)k/((j+1)(n-k))$. It is at least $1$ if and only if $j\le k-1+k/n$. Since $0<k/n<1$, the ratio is at least $1$ exactly for $j\le k-1$. So $t_k$ is the maximum.

steps.slogan: Bound $\binom nk$ from below, and then get the tail bound.
steps.detail: The $n+1$ terms sum to $1$ and each is at most $t_k$. So $1\le(n+1)\binom nk2^{-nH(p)}$. For the tail, $P(X\le k)=2^{-n}\sum_{j\le k}\binom nj\le2^{-n(1-H(k/n))}$.

concepts.c:entropy: The entropy gives the exponent in all three bounds.
concepts.c:binomial-distribution: The tail bound is a statement about the binomial distribution.
concepts.c:binomial-coefficient: The coefficients are the terms that we sum and bound.

statement: Let $X$ be a complex [Banach space](c:banach-space), $T$ a [compact operator](c:compact-operator) on $X$, and $\mu\ne0$. Then exactly one case holds. Either $\mu$ is an [eigenvalue](c:eigenvalue) of $T$, or $\mu-T$ is bijective with bounded inverse. So $\mu-T$ is injective if and only if it is surjective.

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is complete, and the proof uses this to show that ranges are closed.
The operator $T$ maps bounded sets to relatively compact sets.
The scalar $\mu$ is nonzero. For $\mu=0$ the statement fails.

conclusion: Either $\ker(\mu-T)\ne\{0\}$, or $\mu-T$ is bijective with bounded inverse. So every nonzero point of the spectrum is an eigenvalue.

formal.difference: The declaration is a neighbouring mathlib fact. It states a related or smaller result in the form that mathlib uses.

proofs.name: Riesz lemma against compactness
proofs.slogan: Show that an injective $\mu-T$ is bounded below and has closed ranges, then use the Riesz lemma and compactness to rule out strict chains.
proofs.scope: The dichotomy for $\mu\ne0$, with the equivalence of injectivity and surjectivity.

roles.why: Completeness makes the range of a bounded below operator closed.
Compactness gives convergent subsequences of $Tx_n$, and rules out a sequence with $\|Ty_n-Ty_m\|\ge|\mu|/2$.
A nonzero $\mu$ lets us divide by $\mu$ and gives the separation $|\mu|/2$.

steps.slogan: If $\mu-T$ is injective, show that it is bounded below.
steps.detail: Suppose not, so there are unit vectors $x_n$ with $Sx_n\to0$ for $S=\mu-T$. A subsequence has $Tx_{n_k}\to y$, so $x_{n_k}\to y/\mu=:x$ with $\|x\|=1$ and $Sx=0$. This contradicts injectivity.

steps.slogan: Show that the ranges $V_n=S^n(X)$ are closed and decrease.
steps.detail: Each $S^n$ is injective and bounded below. On a complete space, such an operator has closed range: if $S^nx_k$ converges, then $x_k$ is Cauchy and its limit $x$ has $S^nx$ as the limit. So $V_{n+1}\subseteq V_n$ are closed.

steps.slogan: Show that an injective $S$ is surjective, by the Riesz lemma and compactness.
steps.detail: If $V_1\ne X$, the chain $V_n$ is strictly decreasing since $S^n$ is injective. The Riesz lemma gives unit vectors $y_n\in V_n$ with $\operatorname{dist}(y_n,V_{n+1})\ge1/2$. For $m>n$, $Ty_n-Ty_m=\mu(y_n-z)$ with $z\in V_{n+1}$, so $\|Ty_n-Ty_m\|\ge|\mu|/2$. This contradicts compactness.

steps.slogan: Show that a surjective $S$ is injective, with the kernels $\ker S^n$.
steps.detail: If $Sx_1=0$ with $x_1\ne0$, surjectivity gives $x_{k+1}$ with $Sx_{k+1}=x_k$. So the kernels $K_n=\ker S^n$ strictly increase. The Riesz lemma gives unit $y_n\in K_n$ with $\operatorname{dist}(y_n,K_{n-1})\ge1/2$, and the same estimate contradicts compactness.

steps.slogan: Combine the parts to get the alternative and the bounded inverse.
steps.detail: If $\mu$ is not an eigenvalue, $S$ is injective, hence bijective, and bounded below by $c$, so $\|S^{-1}y\|\le\|y\|/c$. If $\mu$ is an eigenvalue, $S$ is not injective. So exactly one case holds.

concepts.c:banach-space: Completeness gives closed ranges for bounded below operators.
concepts.c:compact-operator: Compactness rules out the separated sequence that the Riesz lemma builds.
concepts.c:eigenvalue: The alternative says that the failure of injectivity is an eigenvalue.
